list.listitem: For most, type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) presents abruptly over several days to weeks with the classic triad of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Under 2 years of age, however, the presentation is more likely to be atypical and progress to moderate to severe diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). C
Patients with T1DM are best treated with a team approach to include a primary physician, an endocrinologist, a nutritionist, a mental health specialist, and a nurse educator. C
Intensive insulin therapy with either multiple daily injections (MDI) or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII or "insulin pump") is the standard treatment for T1DM. A
Glycemic goals should be as close to normal as possible while minimizing hypoglycemia. C

Cardiovascular disease prevention is recommended for many patients with T1DM and may include statin, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE-I), and/or aspirin therapy, depending on other patient-specific factors. A

background.definition: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) results from an autoimmune process that destroys the pancreatic beta cells, ultimately leading to an absolute deficiency of insulin secretion.

list.listitem: In the United States and worldwide, T1DM incidence is rising.
In the United States, T1DM incidence was 21.7 new cases per 100,000 per year in those under 20 years old from 2002 to 2012.
Approximately 30% of T1DM patients develop symptoms after age 18.

T1DM occurs in both children and adults. In children, hallmark symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia are typical and approximately one-third present with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In adults, presentation with T1DM may be more variable.
The etiology, which remains unkown, is due to a combination of environmental and genetic factors.

Genetics plays a multifactorial role: identical twins have a 30% to 70% concordance rate; HLA DR3 and HLA DR4 are involved on multiple loci; and first degree relatives of a non-twin sibling or a parent with T1DM have a risk of 3% to 4% or 5% to 15%, respectively, of developing T1DM.

Genetic associations include HLA DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8; these are present in 90% of children with T1DM. HLA DR15-DQ6 is found in less than 1% of those with T1DM, and in more than 20% of the general population and is considered to be protective against T1DM.
Viral infections are a possible environmental contributor and include enteroviruses, coxsackievirus B, cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, and mumps.

Another possible environmental contributor is the hygiene hypothesis, which states that lack of early exposure to illness creates an imbalance in the immune system, upsetting the body's balance and thus placing the child at risk for development of T1DM.
The role of gut microbiota is another possible environmental contributor to the development of T1DM.
Type of infant formula is not associated with increased risk of T1DM.
Use of cephalosporins, penicillins, and macrolides during the first four years of life is not associated with the formation of T1DM autoantibodies.
Beta cells are responsible for producing insulin. Various genetic and environmental factors result in progressive loss of beta cell function and therefore progressive insulin deficiency.
As beta cell destruction progresses, glucose regulation becomes increasingly impaired, and clinical T1DM develops.

There are now thought to be three distinct stages of T1DM: In Stage 1, patients have autoantibodies present, but have not yet developed symptoms or dysglycemia. In Stage 2, glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels have risen, but patients remain asymptomatic. In Stage 3, patients have become symptomatic and frankly hyperglycemic, and diagnosis is made by standard criteria (see Diagnosis section below).

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Inconsistent results, including opposing effect directions and varying effect sizes, make it difficult to comment meaningfully here. Family history may increase the risk slightly.

Patients should receive all usual childhood immunizations, and children >6 months and adults should receive injected influenza vaccine annually. Additionally, vaccination with 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is recommended for those 2 months to 2 years; those 2 to 64 years old should receive 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV), and for those over 65 an additional dose of PPSV is recommended. Finally, hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for adults 19 to 59 years old and considered for those 60 and older. C

Patients with T1DM between 40 and 75 years of age and who do not have athersclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) should receive moderate-intensity statin therapy, and all patients with T1DM who have ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD risk >20% should receive high-intensity statin therapy. A Those with T1DM greater than 75 years old and no ASCVD should receive moderate-intensity statin therapy. B Those with T1DM under 40 years old with at least one additional ASCVD risk factor should consider moderate-intensity statin therapy. C

While the ADA standards of care recommend consideration of daily aspirin for primary prevention of ASCVD among adults with T1DM age 50 or older and at least one additional ASCVD risk factor, C a more recent recommendation from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association recommends consideration of low dose aspirin for those age 40 to 70 with increased risk of ASCVD and without increased risk of bleeding (best justified for those with 10-year ASCVD risk >10% who do not achieve optimal targets for other ASCVD risk factors such as lipids, blood pressure, and glycemia). A Additionally, routine low dose aspirin is not recommended for primary prevention for those older than 70 years or at any age if they have known increased risk of bleeding. A In those with T1DM and a history of ASCVD, daily aspirin 75 to 162 mg should be used for secondary prevention of ASCVD. A

For patients with T1DM and ASCVD, consider ACE-I or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) therapy for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events. B For patients with T1DM and chronic kidney disease (CKD), use of an ACE-I or ARB does not appear to decrease all-cause mortality or cardiovascular death, but may decrease the incidence of kidney failure, based on low quality data. B
See for general screening recommendations for patients with T1DM.
Screening the general population for immune markers to identify at risk individuals for development of T1DM is not recommended.

Screening with a panel of islet autoantibodies should be offered to first degree relatives of those with type 1 diabetes in the setting of clinical research studies, in order to enable diagnosis at an earlier (preclinical) stage.
In patients already diagnosed with T1DM, screening for complications is important: diabetic nephropathy, diabetic retinopathy, diabetic neuropathy, and cardiovascular disease.
Screening for celiac disease should be considered at or shortly after diagnosis with T1DM, 2 to 5 years after diagnosis, and in those who develop celiac symptoms thereafter.B I

In patients with T1DM who have no symptoms suspicious for celiac disease, the cutoff values for celiac serologies may need to be further optimized to improve test characteristics. A genetic testing strategy involving HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 might be useful for screening for celiac disease in patients with T1DM, as a negative result is generally reassuring against the presence of celiac disease (more than 90% of patients with celiac have either HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8).

Autoimmune thyroid disease is also associated with T1DM, with 17% to 30% of patients with T1DM developing some form of thyroid dysfunction. In some small studies, subclinical thyroid disease is associated with hypoglycemic events and decreased linear growth. Thus, most expert panels recommend screening every 1 to 2 years with a TSH. C
Screening for asymptomatic bacteruria in patients with diabetes is not recommended.

Statin therapy to reduce risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or cardiovascular events: Add high-intensity statin therapy to lifestyle therapy for patients of all ages with 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk >20% or if personal history of ASCVD. A Consider moderate-intensity statin therapy for patients <40 years old with additional ASCVD risk factors. C Add moderate-intensity statin therapy to lifestyle therapy for patients without ASCVD who are 40 to 75 years old A and patients >75 years old. B Consider high-intensity statin therapy for patients with multiple ASCVD risk factors. C Consider additional LDL-lowering therapy for patients on maximally tolerated statin dose if their LDL remains >70 mg/dL. A
Aspirin, 75 to 162 mg daily, may be considered for primary prevention of ASCVD for those with increased cardiovascular risk and without increased risk of bleeding.
Non-smokers should be advised never to start smoking, and patients with T1DM who do smoke should be provided with smoking cessation advice.
Healthy lifestyle practices (including diet, exercise, and weight management) are encouraged for all.
A large double-blind randomized controlled trial of adolescents with T1DM showed no difference in albumin-to-creatinine ratio with statin and ACE inhibitor use.
The anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody teplizumab can delay onset of T1DM by about 2 years.
Children should receive all recommended vaccines. Adults and children 6 months and older should receive influenza vaccine annually.

Vaccination with a four-dose series of the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV-13) is recommended for those 2 months to 2 years; those 2 to 64 years old should receive 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV-23), and for those over 65 an additional dose of PPSV-23 is recommended (at least 5 years after their prior dose).
Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for adults 19 to 59 years old and should be considered for those 60 and older.
COVID-19 vaccination is encouraged and will likely be considered as periodic preventive care in the future.

In patients with known cardiovascular disease, ACE-I or ARB, aspirin 75 to 162 mg/day, and high-potency statin therapy should be used to decrease risk of subsequent cardiovascular events unless there is increased risk of bleeding.

Diabetes diagnosis is based on any two results consistent with the following; this can include each of two different test types on the same sample, each of two different test types on separate samples, or the same test type performed on separate samples, unless there is unequivoval hyperglycemia (in which case a single result can suffice): C Fasting plasma glucose >126 mg/dL Plasma glucose >200 mg/dL 2-hours after ingestion of 75g glucose aqueous solution HbA1c >6.5%, though this is not the preferred test if symptoms have developed rapidly/acutely Random plasma glucose >200 mg/dL in a patient with symptomatic hyperglycemia

Differentiating between immune-mediated T1DM and idiopathic T1DM and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is important for future treatment; the presence of autoantibodies to islet cells, GAD, and/or insulin, or some less common autoantibodies (to tyrosine phosphatases IA-2 and IA-2b, and ZnT8) confirm immune-mediated T1DM. Low C-peptide levels also distinguish T1DM (either autoimmune or idiopathic) from T2DM. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Obesity, ethnicity, and evidence of metabolic syndrome/insulin resistance; specific autoantibodies and C-peptides are not routinely detected

Differential.Differential_Name: Hyperglycemia associated with stress or illness
Differential.Differential_Features: Ketonemia not present, may find precipitating cause (steroids)
Polyuria and polydipsia with orthostasis and dehydration but without significant hyperglycemia
Weight loss but no significant dehydration or hyperglycemia
Prior hx of alcoholism, lower degree of hyperglycemia (tends to be 150-300 mg/dL), alcohol levels may not be elevated since it occurs at the end of a binge
Presents with metabolic acidosis, hx of ingestion, tinnitus, and elevated salicylate level
Later onset; may have slower progression to complete insulin depletion
Classic triad is intermittent headache, sweating, and tachycardia: will get hypertension and hyperglycemia as well: check 24 h urine for VMA/metanephrines
Glucocorticoid excess: obesity, insulin resistance, hirsutism, striae

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: American Diabetes Association diagnostic criteria include any two abnormal results from among the following (any two abnormal results from different samples, or abnormal results from two different test types performed on the same sample or different samples), unless there is unequivocal hyperglycemia, in which case a single abnormal results is sufficient: Fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or greater (7.0 mmol/L). Fasting is defined by 8 hours of no caloric intake. Random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms of hyperglycemia including polyuria, polydipsia, and/or unexplained weight loss. Plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater (11.1 mmol/L) two hours after a 75 g aqueous oral glucose load. HbA1c of 6.5% or greater.

list.listitem: T1DM tends to present rapidly with symptoms over a median of 10 days (range 0-180 days). The classic triad includes polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss.

A prospective cohort study identifying newly diagnosed T1DM cases in Ireland over a period of 2 years reported on 283 cases: 4% were less than 2 years of age, 17% between the ages of 2 and 5 years, 37% between the ages of 5 and 10 years, and 42% between the ages of 10 and 15 years.

In the same study, polyuria and polydipsia were the presenting symptoms in about 70% of children and were absent in only 2% of those patients older than the age of 5 years. Secondary enuresis was reported in nearly 20% of children between the ages of 2 and 10 years. Lethargy was more common in children older than 5 years old (15%-20%), while vomiting was more often reported in infants.
Weight loss is more common in newly diagnosed patients under the age of 2 years or over the age of 10 years (40%), but is seen less often in children between the ages of 2 and 10 years (22%).
Other symptoms may include visual disturbances such as blurring or clouding.

DKA is the presenting symptom for approximately 25% to 30% of newly diagnosed patients with T1DM, but may occur more often in children less than 2 years of age. In this age group presentation is more likely to be moderate to severe DKA and may be more difficult to diagnose. It should be considered as a possibility in children with tachypnea with or without a fever of unknown etiology.
Once diagnosis is suspected, same day referral for immediate care initiation with a multidisciplinary team is recommended.
Typically, the diagnosis of T1DM is straightforward. However, in recent years T2DM has become more common in young people.

Measurement of autoantibodies, including GAD65, IA-2, insulin antibody, and islet cell antibody can be useful. These are present in patients with T1DM approximately 70% to 80%, 32% to 75%, and 10% to 60% of the time, respectively.
If these autoantibodies are absent, measuring C-peptide levels is appropriate. In T1DM, the C-peptide levels will generally be low (<1.2 ng/mL) or, if stimulated, less than 1.8 ng/mL.
Proinsulin split product levels may be measured if doubt remains. One study reported levels of these products twice as high in T2DM as in T1DM.
See for a general overview.
Intensive insulin therapy with either multiple daily injections (MDI) or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) is the standard treatment for T1DM. A

Intensive treatment reduces the risk of microvascular complications, but compared to MDI, CSII can produce moderate improvement in HbA1c and can reduce the risks of diabetic ketoacidosis and hypoglycemia. A
Tight glycemic management with HbA1c <7.0% has been associated with better cardiovascular outcomes, including cardiovascular mortality, in persons with T1DM. A

HbA1c goals should be individualized and re-evaluated periodically. HbA1c goal of <7% is recommended for most people with T1DM. Higher goals (e.g., 7.5 or 8) or lower goals (e.g., in pregnancy) should be considered in certain cases. B

SGLT-2 inhibitors (in particular sotagliflozin and dapagliflozin) have shown potential benefits as adjuvant therapy to insulin for patients with T1DM but have not been approved by the FDA for use in this patient population at this time. B

Frequent self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) and/or continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) should be performed by most adults using MDI or CSII and all children with T1DM, at the following times B: Before eating, including meals and snacks, and accordingly before bolus insulin administration Before going to sleep Before exercise Sometimes after eating When suspecting hypoglycemia After treating hypoglycemia, until hypoglycemia and symptoms have resolved Before critical activities, e.g., driving

Adding continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) to intensive insulin therapy may lower HbA1c in adults and youth not meeting glycemic goals when CGM is used properly. It is especially helpful in patients with frequent hypoglycemic episodes.A
Hybrid closed loop systems may reduce HbA1c levels and increase time in range and should be considered for youth and adults with T1DM. A

Self-management education and support should be provided, along with exercise counseling, an individualized nutrition plan, and integrated psychosocial care. This may involve peers, community health workers, lay health coaches, or patient navigators. Glucagon should be prescribed and its use taught to family and friends. A

Insulin is the mainstay of drug therapy with T1DM (see for options). Initial insulin requirements are typically 0.5 to 1.0 units/kg. Starting at 0.2 to 0.4 units/kg and titrating upward is a safe way to start. About 50% to 70% of the total insulin requirement should be given as long-acting basal insulin. Rapid-acting insulin may be given as boluses, before or with meals/snacks, to make up the remainder. Titrate insulin to blood glucose levels.

A "honeymoon phase" frequently occurs shortly after diagnosis with a reduced need for insulin. During puberty, insulin requirements tend to increase. With the menstrual cycle, insulin requirements may fluctuate, as they may with illness as well.
Most patients with T1DM should receive intensive insulin therapy through multiple daily injections (MDI) or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII).

Using 6 mm needles with angled insertion to the abdomen causes less pain and provides the most reliable delivery of subcutaneous insulin for children and adolescents between the ages of 6 and 14 years.
An individualized nutrition plan is recommended for all people with T1DM, preferably developed with and provided by a registered dietician.
Carbohydrate counting of all food and drink is required to match carbohydrate intake to insulin dosages in fixed dosage regimens or to calculate insulin doses in flexible regimens.

HbA1c goals are individually determined based on age and hypoglycemic risk. For non-pregnant adults, HbA1c goals of <7.0 are reasonable in the absence of significant hypoglycemia. For children and adolescents, HbA1c goal of <7.5% is recommended.

Basal (long-acting) insulins in MDI regimens. Studies comparing glargine and detemir insulin are mixed with regard to hypoglycemic episodes, overall glycemia, and weight gain. Overall they are at least as effective as NPH with a similar safety profile. However, NPH insulin has also been associated with less hypoglycemia and greater HbA1c improvement than the long acting analogs glargine and detemir, at less than half the cost.

A meta-analysis of trials including more than 14,000 adult patients showed benefits for use of ultra long-acting and long-acting insulin over intermediate-acting insulin in terms of improved glycemia, reduced weight gain, and reduced risk of hypoglycemia.

Rapid-acting insulin analogs (lispro, glulisine, aspart) are recommended for most patients with T1DM, as they more closely approximate physiologic insulin action and reduce risk of hypoglycemia. They are typically used in used in combination with a long-acting insulin in MDI regimens, or as the only insulin in CSII, as the insulin pump delivers it on demand for boluses and continuously for basal needs.

Most people with T1DM should receive CSII or MDI. The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT)/Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications study concluded that intensive therapy results in a modest reduction in long-term mortality and morbidity due to cardiovascular disease.This mortality reduction was maintained at 27 years' mean follow-up. In one RCT, CSII reduced severe hypoglycemia and DKA, and patients had lower daily insulin requirements compared to MDI, but no overall improvement in glycemia.Two meta-analyses on this same topic showed modest improvement in HbA1c levels (0.4%-0.6%) with CSII. In addition, hypoglycemic events were significantly reduced with CSII, but adverse events, such as DKA, were too few to offer comment. A Cochrane review supports these conclusions. CSII is better received by patients and parents on quality of life indicators than MDI therapy.

Recommended testing frequencies are high, around eating, insulin dosing, exercise, bedtime, and other events such as driving. Meeting these testing and frequency recommendations can be challenging across age groups, but especially among adolescents. Efforts to increase self-monitoring blood glucose (SMBG) efforts have had mixed results. A recent RCT demonstrated that a modest daily financial incentive for adolescents with T1DM improved SMBG frequency and glycemia compared to no incentive (combined endpoint of testing >4 times/day with >1 result in target range, 50.0% vs. 18.9%). Once the incentive was discontinued, target behaviors returned to baseline (15.3% and 8.7%).

Adding continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) to intensive insulin therapy may lower HbA1c in adults and youth not meeting glycemic goals when CGM is used properly. It is especially helpful in patients with frequent hypoglycemic episodes. SMBG and/or CGM use should be frequent, as higher SMBG frequency and higher CGM sensor use frequency have both been correlated with greater degrees of HbA1c lowering.

Recent studies demonstrated that the use of real-time CGM lowered HbA1c and increased time in range in adolescents and young adults. One example is a RCT of 153 participants 14 to 24 years of age that showed a significant lowering of HbA1c from baseline to 26 weeks of at least 0.5% in 44% of the CGM group vs. 21% of the control group (P = .005). Another randomized trial of 149 patients with T1DM compared CGM with capillary blood glucose testing, and found less episodes of hypoglycemia (NNT = 4) and fewer requiring intervention by a third party (NNT = 4).
Another study of 156 participants with HgbA1C of 7.5% to 11.0% found that those randomized to intermittently scanned CGM had lower HgbA1C and more time in range than the group using SMBG.

"Closed loop artificial pancreas systems" which automate insulin delivery by integrating CSII and CGM with a computerized controller, can improve glycemia (by reducing hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, or both, depending on the automation features present in a given system) and should be considered for therapeutic use. Other RCTs have also demonstrated benefit of the bihormonal bionic pancreas with use of a weight based algorithm to achieve adaptive meal priming boluses, demonstrating its utility in patients with variable insulin requirements, increasing blood glucose time in range, decreasing hyperglycemia while also decreasing hypoglycemia, and decreasing the amount of work required by the patient, including carbohydrate counting, bolus calculations, and basal and bolus adjustments.
Open source automated insulin delivery systems have been developed and are also effective.

A similar closed-loop insulin-only system significantly reduced nocturnal hypoglycemia in a recent RCT, as did a hybrid closed-loop insulin-only system among a wide age range of patients with suboptimal glycemia in T1DM. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs of closed loop artificial pancreas systems found them to be safe and effective compared to standard therapy, with increased time in near normoglycemia, and decreased time in hypoglycemia both overnight and throughout the 24 hour day.

There have been a few randomized trials of closed-loop systems in children. A recent RCT demonstrated 2.6 hours less per day in hyperglycema among children 6-13 years old using a closed-loop system. A second study randomized 102 children 2 to 6 years of age to a closed-loop system for 13 weeks. The mean time within range was higher by the end of the study period (69.3% vs 55.9%, p < .001). Hybrid closed loop systems may also have benefit in decreasing time below range (time in hypoglycemia) and increasing quality of life among children.
Hypoglycemia is a significant barrier to achieving optimal glycemic targets in T1DM. It is important to inquire about the occurrence and severity of hypoglycemic events at every visit.

15 to 20 g of glucose is preferred for the treatment of mild hypoglycemia (most frequent), with reassessment of glucose level by SMBG 15 minutes after treatment, and if still hypoglycemic, repeating this cycle of treatment and reassessement until hypoglcemia resolves.

Glucagon should be prescribed and its use taught to family and friends. Its availability should be ensured and known at home, school, work, and outings, for the treatment of hypoglycemia in case the patient with T1DM is unwilling or unable (e.g., unconscious) to ingest carbohydrates orally. Recent advances in glucagon availability now include more convenient options: a prefilled syringe for injection, an auto-injector pen, and an intranasal powder. More cumbersome rescue kits remain available, as do a glucagon rescue kit training app for smartphones, which can be helpful.
A small crossover RCT recently demonstrated safety and efficacy of mini-dose glucagon (15%-30% of the standard emergency kit dose) in the treatment of non-severe hypoglycemia.

Pramlintide is an adjunctive therapy given with meals to reduce postprandial hyperglycemia in patients with T1DM not achieving glycemic goals with insulin and diet therapy alone. The effect on clinical outcomes is unknown. A small randomized controlled trial conducted in Canada in 2020 showed potential improvements in glycemia with use of a rapid insulin-and-pramlintide artificial pancreas compared to a rapid insulin-alone artificial pancreas.
Other medications indicated for the treatment of T2DM are being studied in the treatment of T1DM, with variable results.

SGLT-2 inhibitors have shown potential benefits as adjuvant therapy to insulin in patients with T1DM, including improved glycemia, decrease in total daily insulin dosing, and weight loss. However, use of these medications can increase the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, though further characterization of the magnitude of this risk is needed.

A meta-analysis of RCTs of sotagliflozin in T1DM found impoved glycemic outcomes (weighted mean difference attributed to sotagliflozin -0.34% for HbA1c, -16.98 mg/dL for fasting plasma glucose, and -39.2 mg/dL for two-hour post-prandial plasma glucose). Similar benefits were found for dapagliflozin as adjuvant therapy to insulin in patients with T1DM in another large international RCT, though the rates of DKA were similar across the moderate therapy and control groups (a definitive diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis was made in 1% of patients in the dapagliflozin 5 mg group, 2% of patients in the dapagliflozin 10 mg group, and 1% in the placebo group). A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to evaluate the efficacy and safety of SGLT-2 inhibitors among patients with T1DM and chronic kidney disease (CKD).

The GLP-1 receptor agonists liraglutide and exenatide have been studied as an adjunctive therapy to insulin in patients with T1DM. The largest trials were done with liraglutide (in addition to insulin vs. placebo in addition to insulin) in the ADJUNCT ONE (nearly 1,400 patients) and ADJUNCT TWO (835 patients) trials. At liraglutide doses of 1.2 mg and 1.8 mg, patients in the intervention arm in both trials experienced statistically significant decreases in weight, total daily insulin dose, and A1c, but there was also a significant increase in the rate of hypoglycemia in the liraglutide treatment groups (along with an increase in ketosis found with liraglutide 1.8 mg).

A smaller RCT evaluated addition of metformin for children with T1DM aged 8 to 18 years, and found HbA1c to be 1.0% lower in the metformin group compared to the placebo group during the 12 month study (P = .001), with decreased total daily insulin dose in the metformin group (−0.2 units/kg/day, P = .001).
See Type 2 diabetes chapter for treatment management and insulin therapy initiation.

Physical activity is a cornerstone of lifestyle management and for most adults with T1DM should include at least 150 minutes/week of vigorous aerobic activity, involving at least 3 days/week, with no more than 2 consecutive days without such activity. Shorter durations (at least 75 minutes/week) may be appropriate for some, especially younger and more physically fit people with T1DM. Muscle-strengthening and/or bone-strengthening activities should be included. Insulin and/or nutrition adjustment should be considered in the context of physical activity, as glycemic response to exercise can be variable. C

In the athlete, insulin absorption is affected by temperature. Heat or cold modalities such as ice or hot tubs will affect injection sites. Therefore, avoid ice packs over injection sites and hot tubs for 1 to 3 hours after injections. Avoidance of hypo/hyperglycemia is key.
Glucose intake requirements for exercise may increase up to moderate intensity exercise but have not been shown to be increased for high intensity exercise.
See recommendations in for insulin management recommendations.
Diabetes education is a cornerstone for initial care and during follow-up visits to assist long-term success.

Social context should be assessed and considered as treatment decisions are made. Such considerations should include inequities and social determinants of health (such as food insecurity, housing stability or homelessness, language, financial, and cultural barriers, and community support).

Self-management support should be provided when available, and may involve peers (in-person and/or online), community health workers, lay health coaches, or patient navigators. Advocacy activities can also be useful in promoting perceived self-efficacy.

Social context should be assessed and considered as treatment decisions are made. Such considerations should include inequities and social determinants of health (such as food insecurity, housing stability or homelessness, language, financial barriers, health literacy and cultural barriers, and community support).

People with T1DM have an increased risk of psychosocial distress and psychiatric disorders, including diabetes distress, fear of hypoglycemia, depression, and anxiety, as well as issues related to social adjustment and work/school performance. Routine screening and treatment or referral as indicated should be accomplished. Consider starting assessments for psychosocial and diabetes distress around 7 to 8 years of age.
During adolescence, behavioral family systems therapy may improve communication and problem solving skills in the family unit and improve long-term glycemia.

Consider screening for eating disorders and disordered eating behaviors among people with T1DM between 10 to 12 years of age. Patients might reduce or omit insulin as a weight loss technique considered a disordered eating behavior, leading to poorer glycemia, especially among adolescents. The Diabetes Eating Problems Survey-Revised (DEPS-R) can be used to screen for disturbed eating behaivors.
Motivational interviewing in adolescent patients can facilitate behavior change and improve overall glycemia.

Technology use, such as web-based intervention or text messaging, is a cost-effective method to help adolescents communicate with their healthcare team and transition to adult healthcare systems. More studies are needed to determine long term benefits of these programs.

There may be a point when attitude changes and the patient decides to "get serious" about treating their diabetes. This "conversion" can occur suddenly as they become aware of the threat that diabetes has on their health. They may seek specialist care if they feel their primary physician is not attentive to this attitude shift.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 36 prospective, controlled studies found that behavioral programs improved HbA1c for up to 6 months post-intervention, with insufficient evidence for any other outcomes.

Stem cells can be differentiated into insulin-secreting beta cells and glucagon-secreting alpha cells. Researchers developed zimislecel (VX-880) which consists of allogeneic stem cell–derived islets. In a small phase 1/2 study, they succesfully resulted in insulin independence for 10 of 12 patients.

Clinical trials with pancreatic islet cell transplantation have shown short-term efficacy, but more research is needed to evaluate long term benefits and to fully understand safety concerns. The need for multiple transplants and relatively low rates of insulin independence (˜20%) are limitations.

Medical nutritional therapy is a key component to diabetes management. Low-glycemic index diets have some beneficial effects on intermediate outcomes. Appropriately timing insulin with carbohydrate intake may successfully bring HbA1c levels down an additional 1% to 2%.
Fiber intake should be 25 to 50 g daily or 15 to 25 g/1000 kcal ingested.
Protein intake should be restricted for patients with CKD.

A Cochrane review, based on low-certainty evidence, supports salt intake reduction to less than 5 gm/day (2 gm sodium) to lower systolic and diastolic blood pressures for patients with T1DM regardless of the presence or absence of hypertension or CKD. Salt reduction has a similar magnitude of effect to drug monotherapy for hypertension among patients with T1DM.

Certain religious faiths hold specific safety challenges for the patient with T1DM, especially around practices involving food restriction such as fasts. For the Muslim patient, Ramadan involves fasting for a prolonged period. Expert derived guidelines have been devised to assist.Consensus from the South Asian Health Foundation recommends against fasting during Ramadan for Muslim patients with T1DM. If a patient chooses to do so, checking sugars frequently (at least 4 times per day or with continuous monitoring), is recommended, along with careful insulin adjustments.
All people with diabetes should have available integrated, collaborative psychosocial care in order to optimize health outcomes and quality of life. A

A Cochrane review, based on moderate-certainty evidence, noted the efficacy of periodontal treatment using subgingival instrumentation in improving glycemic control among patients with T1DM with periodontal disease.
Treatment is lifelong with careful attention not only to glycemia but also to cardiovascular risk factors and prevention of complications including neuropathy, nephropathy, and retinopathy.
Consider referring children with T1DM to a multidisciplinary team of specialists experienced in diabetes management in children and adolescents.
Referral to an eye care specialist for regular dilated eye examination is recommended; telemedicine programs with validated retinal photography may be considered.
Consult a nephrologist when glomerular filtration rate falls below 30, or with questions about cause, rapid progression, or difficulty managing renal disease.
Consider referral to a podiatrist and/or vascular surgeon for nonhealing ulcer.
See for management of hypoglycemia.

In those with hypoglycemia unawareness or for anyone following a significant hypoglycemic event, glycemic targets should be raised for at least several weeks in order to reduce risk of subsequent hypoglycemia and to allow partial reversal of hypoglycemia unawareness. A

Frequent and severe hypoglycemia has been associated with cognitive dysfunction, and hypoglycemia becomes more difficult to identify and therefore poses increased risk when cognition is low or declining.
See chapter on diabetic ketoacidosis for its management.
An intact vascular supply is the best indicator for success for wound healing.Regular inspection of the legs and feet with early intervention when needed is important to prevent ulceration.

Achieving and maintaining blood pressure and glycemic targets are central to treatment and to decrease risk of developing diabetic neuropathy and nephropathy. ACE-I are the only class of antihypertensive agents to independently show a reduction in the development of microalbuminuria.
Microalbuminuria alone may not predict renal failure.

A Cochrane review concluded that for patients with T1DM and chronic kidney disease (CKD), ACE-I or ARB does not appear to decrease all-cause mortality or cardiovascular death, but may decrease the incidence of kidney failure, based on low quality data.
See chapter on diabetic retinopathy, diabetic neuropathy, and diabetic nephropathy for further details regarding their management.
Macrovascular complications such as cardiovascular disease must also be managed, mainly through risk factor reduction (see Screening and Prevention section).
Women with T1DM have a higher rate of urinary incontinence than women without diabetes (8.8% vs. 4.5% in NHANES cohort); screening and management should be considered.

Key principles to sick day management can be found in the ISPAD Clinical Practice Guidelines. Fluids with carbohydrates to maintain hydration are crucial for successful sick day management. Mini-dose glucagon may be needed to treat hypoglycemia with nausea. When vomiting occurs, it is important to consider insulin deficiency as a cause until proven otherwise.

When patients are ill, the insulin dose may need adjustment up or down but should never be stopped. Frequent blood glucose monitoring is mandatory: typically every 3 to 4 hours, but may be required as much as every 1 to 2 hours. Home measurements of blood 3-hydroxybutyrate enables earlier detection and treatment of ketosis compared with urine ketone measurements, decreasing emergency room visits and hospitalizations (NNT = 3).

With moderate to large ketones and blood glucose levels over 250 mg/dL, there is a significant risk for DKA. Refer for emergency care or hospitalization if blood sugars continue to rise 2 hours after treatment begins or if there are persistent ketones, unclear diagnosis, worsening dehydration, parental exhaustion, or concomitant illness.
Specialized treatment teams have been shown to improve glycemia and reduce readmission within 3 months. Their impact on quality of life or overall wellbeing has not been evaluated.

One study suggested reduced mortality with tight glycemic management only on surgical ICU patients. However, a recent meta-analysis concluded that there is no all-cause mortality reduction from tight glycemic management for any ICU patients and there is considerable risk from hypoglycemia. In one large multicentered trial, tighter glycemic management (80-108 mg/dL) vs. a less stringent target (<181 mg/dL) for patients with diabetes in the ICU was associated with increased mortality. Insulin therapy should be used in hospitalized patients with persistent glycemia >180 mg/dL to maintain a target glucose of 140 to 180mg/dL in most cases. A
Hypoglycemia in hospitalized patients with diabetes cared for on a general ward was associated with increased inpatient and outpatient mortality and increased length of stay.

Rapid-acting insulin should be used for prandial and correction doses, using a sliding scale, for non-critically ill patients. Use of sliding scale (correction) insulin alone is strongly discouraged. Glucose testing should precede meals, along with prandial insulin administration, in patients who are eating. Long-acting or basal insulin in addition to short-acting correction bolus insulin is required for all hospitalized T1DM patients. A

When they are hospitalized and/or ill, it is best to maintain CSII patients on their own insulin pump. In case of pump malfunction, or if the patient cannot operate their pump or inform medical and nursing staff on pump operation, substitute insulin administration with pen or syringe injection. The insulin replacement dose should be based on blood glucose level, the presence and level of ketones, and total daily dose of insulin up to 0.1 U/kg.
Surgery presents special challenges for patients with diabetes. See algorithm in for a suggested management strategy.

Life expectancy for people with T1DM has recently increased, as has that of the general population. Therefore, while living longer, those with T1DM still have 10 to 13 years lower life expectancy than the general population. B
When overt nephropathy develops, cardiovascular complications may escalate. B
Encourage regular assessment for complications and associated conditions. C

Untreated, hyperglycemia develops as the insulin levels are insufficient to regulate gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Ketoacids build up from the breakdown of free fatty acids. The patient then develops an anion gap metabolic acidosis and becomes dehydrated. Left untreated, coma and death will follow.

Treated, the natural history is dramatically different, with long-term survival and function more likely when maintaining nearer to normal glycemia. Risks of microvacular and macrovascular complications remain elevated but approach the general population's risks with HbA1c maintained below 7.0%. Lower HbA1c levels increase risk of hypoglycemia, and these factors must be balanced.

Life expectancy for patients with T1DM has consistently been estimated to be 10 to 13 years lower than the general population without T1DM. Recent increases in life expectancy of people with T1DM have been similar to those of the general population. The life expectancy gap decreases with older age: 8 years for those between the ages of 55 and 64 years, and 4 years for those between the ages of 65 and 74 years.
The presence of CKD is associated with higher risk of mortality.
With proper treatment, attention to glycemic management, blood pressure monitoring, and risk factor modification, patients with T1DM can live long and successful lives.

At 30-year follow-up from the DCCT, the cumulative incidence rates of proliferative retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular disease were 50%, 25%, and 14%, respectively; the rates were lower among patients treated with intensive therapy (21%, 9%, and 9%, respectively).
Structured, systems-based driven follow-up (automatic reminders) in office practice can improve glycemic management and mortality.

Assess HbA1c level every 3 months in all children and adolescents, every 3 months in adults with unstable T1DM and/or not meeting glycemic targets, and at least every 6 months in adults with stable T1DM meeting glycemic targets.
At each visit: measure weight, height, BMI, and blood pressure, and perform visual foot inspection and skin examination (including injection/infusion set sites, lipodystrophy).

Annually, order lipid profile, hepatic profile, urine albumin:creatinine ratio, serum TSH, serum creatinine with estimated GFR; refer for dilated retinal examination; and perform thyroid palpation and comprehensive foot examination (assessing circulation and sensation in addition to visual foot inspection).

Get and wear a medical ID (e.g., bracelet or pendant). Also consider carrying medical information and emergency contact information for emergency care and first responders (e.g., wallet card and/or smartphone emergency information).
If you use tobacco products, stop. If you do not use tobacco products, do not start.
Exercise daily or almost daily and maintain a healthy weight.
If overweight, initiate plan to lose 5% to 10% of body weight as an initial goal.
Know signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia.
Carry a snack (ideally a source of rapid acting glucose) and glucagon kit. Teach family and friends how to use the glucagon kit.

Consensus from the South Asian Health Foundation recommends against fasting during Ramadan for Muslim patients with T1DM. If a patient chooses to do so, checking sugars frequently (at least 4 times per day), is recommended, along with careful insulin adjustments.

Preconception counseling should be part of routine T1DM care starting at puberty for all girls of child-bearing potential, with discussion of family planning and contraception prescription until ready for pregnancy. A This counseling should include maintaining preconception HbA1c <6.5%, if safely possible, to reduce risk of congenital anomalies. B

Diabetic retinopathy may develop and/or progress during pregnancy. A dilated eye examination is recommended before pregnancy, or in the first trimester if not done before pregnancy. Patients should follow closely with their eye care provider throughout the remainder of their pregancy and for 1 year post-partum. B
In addition to routine prenatal care that is recommended for all pregnant women, those with T1DM should also have HbA1c, TSH, serum creatinine, as well as urine albumin:creatinine ratio.
Refer to a specialty multidisciplinary center for pregnancy care if possible as soon pregnancy is identified.
Some medications frequently used in the treatment of diabetes and its complications are contraindicated in pregnancy (e.g., ACE-I, ARBs, and statins).
During pregnancy, optimal glucose targets should include fasting glucose goal of <95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial glucose goal of <140 mg/dL, and 2-hour postprandial glucose goal <120 mg/dL.

HbA1c target during pregnancy should be tailored to prevent significant hypoglycemia. A target of <6.0% is optimal if it can be achieved without undue risk of significant hypoglycemia, but may be adjusted to <7.0% to prevent hypoglycemia, if needed. B
From the end of the first trimester until delivery, women with T1DM should be prescribed low-dose daily aspirin to decrease the risk of preeclampsia. A

Continuous glucose monitoring and CGM metrics can be used in pregnancy but should not replace self-monitoring of blood glucose to achieve optimal glycemic targets. When used as an adjunct, CGM can help to achieve A1c targets in diabetes and pregnancy. B Continuous glucose monitoring in pregnant women with T1DM can improve neonatal outcomes such by reducing macrosomia, neonatal intensive care admissions greater than 24h, neonatal hypoglycemia, and length of stay. algorithm.title: Overall Approach to Patient with Suspected T1DM.

cell.label: Suspect T1DM due to abrupt onset polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss. Fasting glucose ≥126, casual glucose ≥200 mg/dL, or abnormal glucose tolerance test?
Repeat testing on another day. Abnormal?
Monitor patient, repeat testing if symptomatic.
Same day referral for care and education. Diagnosis of T1DM clear?
Type 1 diabetes. Treat with intensive insulin therapy (multiple daily injections or continuous insulin infusion). Optimize cardiovascular risk factors. A1C at goal for age?
Consider postprandial hyperglycemia (pramlintide may be helpful), adherence, depression, and eating disorders.
Keep at least quarterly follow-up during medication changes.
Check diabetes autoantibodies (GAD65) and basal and/or stimulated C-peptide. Positive GAD65 and low C-peptide?
Highly suggestive of T2DM. Treat as appropriate.
T1DM patient needs surgery. Schedule as first case in morning if possible.
1-2 wk prior to surgery, assess glycemic management? Is it adequate for age?
Preoperative management based on regimen.
Expected duration of surgery >2 h?
Continue pump.
Start glucose-insulin infusion for surgery.

Hold breakfast, check morning glucose. If the blood glucose level is >250, use the insulin correction factor to calculate the necessary insulin dose for correction to 100-200 range. Insulin correction factor: take 1500 and divide by patient's total daily insulin requirement. That is the amount 1 unit of insulin will decrease the blood glucose level. For example, if a patient's total daily dose of insulin is 50 units, it takes 1 unit of insulin to decrease her surgar by 30 mg/dL.
Day of surgery: No short-acting insulin. Give any basal insulin as scheduled.

Adjust regimen prior to clearance.

feature.caption: Management of Symptomatic Hypoglycemia in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
feature.feature_body:
Severity Possible Common Symptoms Treatment
Mild (<70 mg/dL) Diaphoresis, pallor, palpitations, tremor, headache 15 g of carbohydrates (preferably glucose); Recheck glucose level 15 minutes after treatment; repeat treatment if indicated
Moderate Above plus aggressiveness, drowsiness, or confusion 20-30 g of carbohydrates (preferably glucose); Recheck glucose level 15 minutes after treatment; repeat treatment if indicated
Severe (unable to help self, or unwilling or unable to swallow) Above plus altered consciousness, coma, or seizure Glucagon 30 mcg/kg up to 1 mg (nausea likely in 5-15 min); Recheck glucose level 15 minutes after treatment; repeat treatment if indicated
Data from Silverstein J, Klingensmith G, Copeland K. Care of children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes Care 2005;28:186–212.

feature.caption: Managing Insulin in Patients Planning High-Intensity Exercise for At Least 30 Min.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Action
Before exercise Check glucose: <100 mg/dL: snack >250 mg/dL fasting: if ketones positive, do not exercise. If negative, hydrate and exercise cautiously >300 not fasting: exercise with caution, hydrate, and monitor sugars closely
If continuous insulin infusion Decrease basal rate 20%-50% about 1-2 h before exercise. Decrease bolus up to 50% at meals before activity. Suspend pump for up to 60 min at start of exercise. Decrease evening meal bolus by 50% to prevent nocturnal hypoglycemia
If multiple daily injections Decrease bolus dose up to 50% at meal prior to exercise. Decrease evening meal bolus by 50% to prevent nocturnal hypoglycemia
After exercise Check sugar frequently to look for hypoglycemia A snack is acceptable, but insulin adjustment is preferred to calorie increase
Data from Jimenez CC, Corcoran MH, Crawley JT, et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association position statement: management of the athlete with type 1 diabetes mellitus. J Athl Train 2007;42:536–545.
